rationale: This is essentially the published decomposition of the asset-growth anomaly by financing source (Cooper–Gulen–Schill combined with the debt-issuance/external-financing anomaly of Spiess–Affleck-Graves and Bradshaw–Richardson–Sloan), and the rank-product form is also fragile if RANK is zero-centered, since two low ranks would produce a high product and invert the intended ordering.

Total accruals (ib − oancf) are mechanically a large component of asset growth, so this multiplies two heavily overlapping and individually well-documented anomalies (Sloan accruals × asset growth) rather than combining distinct information, and the interaction is likely to be close to a squared version of a single underlying construct.

The expression is internally inconsistent with the stated hypothesis because asset growth can be negative, so the 2× multiplier also doubles the *shrinking* cash-burners' signal in the opposite direction, and using raw unranked GROWTH(at,1) leaves the signal outlier-dominated while adding little beyond the plain asset-growth factor.

Conditioning the investment effect on multi-year ROA volatility is an economically coherent and not-directly-published interaction, though earnings volatility overlaps heavily with distress/idiosyncratic-volatility screens and the 5-year window will cost coverage, so the incremental content over asset growth alone needs to be demonstrated.

Inventory growth relative to sales growth paired with deteriorating gross margin is almost exactly two of the Abarbanell–Bushee fundamental signals (and Thomas–Zhang inventory growth), and the declared INTERACTION_TYPE "ratio" contradicts the expression, which is an additive rank sum with no conditioning at all.

The long-leg framing — asset growth measured in turnover units and validated by sustained internal cash generation — is a defensible and less-crowded angle, but both legs are Piotroski F-score components so the novelty is in the multiplicative form, which will need the rank convention checked to avoid rewarding the doubly-low corner.
